content: The guideline document was meticulously developed to accurately reflect the discussions and decisions made by the participants. The draft version of the document was electronically distributed to the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and the External Review Group (ERG) for their final review and approval. After the GDG members reviewed and approved the document, it was sent to eight external, independent experts from the ERG who were not involved in the guideline panel for peer review. The WHO Steering Group then evaluated the feedback provided by the peer reviewers to determine which inputs should be incorporated into the final document. Following the meeting and external peer review, the WHO Steering Group made modifications to the document, which were limited to correcting factual errors and improving the language to enhance clarity. The recommendations regarding the choice of antiseptic agent and method of application for preoperative skin preparation for cesarean sections were based on guiding principles and best practices. These principles were agreed upon during the 2015 technical consultation on the prevention and treatment of peripartum infections and were later adopted by the 2020 GDG panel. These principles were derived from expert consensus rather than a systematic process of evidence retrieval, synthesis, and grading. They align with good clinical practice standards aimed at improving care related to the prevention and treatment of infectious morbidities during childbirth. The use of alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate for skin preparation prior to elective or emergency cesarean sections is recommended. The method of application should primarily follow the manufacturer’s instructions, as well as the clinician’s experience and preferences. While there is insufficient evidence to recommend a specific concentration of chlorhexidine gluconate, most trials included in the review used a 2% chlorhexidine gluconate solution in 70% alcohol. It is essential to exclude maternal allergy to alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate before surgery, as it can cause skin irritation even in women without a prior history of allergy. A standard preoperative skin preparation technique appropriate for the intended incision site must be followed. Given the flammability of alcohol, care must be taken to ensure the antiseptic solution is allowed to dry completely by evaporation before the use of diathermy. Drapes should not be saturated with alcohol, and pooling of the solution under the patient must be avoided. Special precautions should be taken during emergency cesarean sections. If chlorhexidine gluconate is unavailable, povidone-iodine may be considered as an alternative antiseptic agent, although it is less effective than alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate. The current recommendation aligns with the 2016 WHO global guidelines on the prevention of surgical site infections, which advocate for the use of alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate solutions for surgical site skin preparation. These recommendations supersede Recommendation No. 17 from the 2015 WHO guidelines on the prevention and treatment of maternal peripartum infections, which was previously considered a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. The dissemination and implementation of these recommendations should involve all stakeholders at international, national, and local levels. It is critical to increase women’s access to maternal healthcare at the community level and strengthen the capacity of healthcare facilities to provide high-quality services and information to all women giving birth. These recommendations should be translated into care packages and programs tailored to the specific needs of each country, healthcare facility, and community. National and subnational subgroups may be established to adapt and implement these recommendations based on existing strategies. This process may involve developing or revising national guidelines or protocols to align with the updated recommendations. Successful implementation depends on well-planned, participatory, and consensus-driven processes. An enabling environment should be created to support the use of these recommendations, including changes in healthcare practitioners’ behavior to adopt evidence-based practices. The recommendations should be adapted into documents and tools suitable for different locations and contexts. Modifications to the recommendations, if necessary, should be explicitly justified. In humanitarian emergencies, the adaptation of these recommendations should consider integration with other response strategies and address the unique needs of women in such settings, including their values and preferences. Context-specific tools may be required to support implementation in these scenarios. Healthcare providers and managers should ensure the availability of alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate wherever cesarean sections are performed. However, the availability of these solutions may be limited in some lowand middle-income countries. Local production may be a more affordable and feasible option, provided adequate quality control measures are in place. Women should be adequately counseled and engaged in shared decision-making regarding the use of antiseptic agents for skin preparation, including potential side effects. The GDG did not identify any significant knowledge gaps that would impact the recommendations. However, several barriers may hinder the effective implementation and scale-up of these recommendations. These include a lack of understanding of the value of alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate among women, families, or communities; insufficient human resources with the necessary training and skills; concerns about the safety of alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate among healthcare personnel and managers; unreliable supply systems; and a lack of systems to monitor the use of antibiotics, antiseptic agents, and antimicrobial resistance. Additionally, effective referral mechanisms and care pathways for women requiring additional care may be lacking. The implementation and impact of these recommendations will be monitored at the health service, country, and regional levels as part of broader efforts to improve maternal and perinatal health outcomes.
